items.title: Mao Zedong and the founding of the People's Republic of China (2/3) | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>From peasants' son to revolutionary leader — Mao Zedong laid the foundation for modern China. This three-part documentary offers an in-depth look at one of the most influential figures of the 20th century. *Part 3 coming soon!*

Part 1: https://youtu.be/dP8dX4Pyzd0
Part 2: https://youtu.be/kml_5jNV0j8
Part 3: Available from 17 October 2026

The legacy of the "founding father" of the People's Republic of China remains deeply controversial. Revered in Europe as a revolutionary icon in the late 1960s, Mao led China to the brink of disaster and ultimately clung to power with a regime of terror. Yet today's leaders in Beijing continue to draw on the cult of Mao. China is now a global power, a transformation that would be difficult to imagine without Mao Zedong.

When Mao Zedong was born in 1893, nothing hinted at his meteoric rise to power. The son of a farming family, he grew up during a period of political instability and profound social upheaval. The 1911 Revolution, which marked the beginning of the end of imperial rule, awakened his mind to politics. At first, Mao had no clear political program. But the Russian Revolution of 1917 introduced him to Marxist ideas, and he soon became a co-founder of the Communist Party of China.

Mao rose steadily through the party ranks as conflict with the nationalist Kuomintang party intensified into a bloody civil war. The devastating retreat that became known as the "Long March" went down in history to become the foundation of the cult of Mao. After World War II, the struggle for power in China continued until Mao and his forces finally reached Beijing.

This three-part series traces Mao Zedong's journey from peasants' son to revolutionary and architect of modern China — from his rural childhood to the founding of the People's Republic to the devastating impact of the Cultural Revolution in the 1960s, which claimed millions of lives.

Archival footage, as well as interviews with historians and eyewitnesses, tell the story of the man who changed China forever.

items.title: Skin: Multitalented and underappreciated | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Our skin connects us to the world while also providing us with a boundary and a layer of protection. It's a biotope, an object of desire, and it allows us to smell the way we do. How can we keep our skin healthy, and heal it when it's unwell?

On average, the skin is around two square meters in area and weighs between five and ten kilograms. For a long time, it was viewed primarily as a covering. But this multitalented organ is much more than that. It provides us with one of our senses, it can draw oxygen directly from the air, and it can even perceive sound waves and odor molecules.

The skin is also a status symbol, with smooth, wrinkle-free skin symbolizing youth, beauty and success. Countless experts offer advice, including recommending anti-aging products containing acids, bases, enzymes, vitamins, or proteins. But only a few cosmetics are truly worth it, says dermatologist Professor Claudia Borelli of the University Hospital in Tübingen, Germany. The same goes for the advice of many skincare influencers, who often promote their own interests on social media. So is it better to think twice before rushing to get cosmetic treatments?

Over the past five years, procedures using Botox and hyaluronic acid have more than doubled. Borelli warns that poorly administered fillers can cause problems for years to come. Nevertheless, the clients of cosmetic doctors are getting younger and younger. Gaming streamer Jasmin Gnu had lip fillers in her early 20s — she now regrets that decision. She tells her fans that they don't have to chase the unattainable aesthetic ideals sold to them by the beauty filters used on social media.

Meanwhile, the skin can also be seen as a window into the soul. Stress can make the skin sick, says psychodermatologist Professor Uwe Gieler. About a quarter of Germans suffer from skin conditions such as atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, acne, or allergies. With the help of an anti-inflammatory diet, new medications and therapy, there's a good chance of healing unhealthy skin.

items.title: I tested Antonin Carême's béchamel sauce (it's not what you think)
items.author: French Cooking Academy
items.content:
<article>Did you know the classic Béchamel sauce you know today isn't the original? in this episode we are diving into a 200-year-old culinary masterpiece: Antonin Carême's The Art of French Cooking in the 19th Century. In this first episode, we explore Carême's foundational list of mother sauces, uncover the true origin of the Béchamel , and make the rich, velvety, original version from scratch. then as a bonus I am using the sauce to make a quick old fashioned traditional chicken fricassée!

Ingredients: 
For the Base Chicken/Veal Stock:
Chicken wings – 500g (chopped and rinsed)
Pork or Veal trimmings / Ham – 100g
Water – to barely cover the meat
Bouquet Garni (Bay leaf, fresh thyme, mushroom, shallot parsley stalks, piece of leek)
Salt and black pepper – to taste

For the Béchamel:
350 ml veal or chicken stock
40 grams Unsalted butter – for the roux and aromatics
Flour (all-purpose) – 30g (for the roux)
Aromatics (Parsley stalks, sliced mushrooms, leek, carrots, celery, shallot )
Lean unsmoked ham or pork pieces – 100g
Heavy cream  200 ml– added in stages for reduction
Freshly grated nutmeg, salt, and black pepper

For the Fricassée Garnish & Finishing:
Fresh chicken breast – seasoned with salt and pepper
White mushrooms – white-cooked with butter, salt, pepper, and lemon juice
Pre-cooked carrots – sliced
Fresh chervil (or parsley) – for garnish

items.title: Why AI Is Sucking Up the World’s Wealth
items.author: Bloomberg Originals
items.content:
<article>Bloomberg Originals unpacks how the artificial intelligence boom has resulted in a concentration of immense wealth. By drawing investment away from emerging markets and traditional industries, this massive capital drain is pushing global trade imbalances to levels unseen since the 2008 financial crisis.

CHAPTERS

items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This interview was recorded for the GOTO Book Club. #GOTOcon #GOTObookclub
http://gotopia.tech/bookclub

Check out more here:
https://gotopia.tech/episodes/455

Garrison Hinson-Hasty - Author of "Systems Programming with Zig" & Contributor to the Zig Compiler
Trevor Berrange Sanchez - Systems Software Engineer & Particularly Fond of Zig

RESOURCES
Garrison
https://github.com/garrisonhh

Trevor
https://www.linkedin.com/in/trevor-berrange-sanchez-035259426

Links
https://youtu.be/YXrb-DqsBNU
https://youtu.be/wFlyUzUVFhw
https://youtu.be/jIZpKpLCOiU

DESCRIPTION
Garrison Hinson-Hasty, author of “Systems Programming with Zig” and a contributor to the Zig compiler, joins Trevor Berrange Sanchez to explain why he wrote a book on a pre-1.0 language that breaks frequently (he's currently updating the last seven chapters for Zig 0.16). His answer: the language's slow march toward 1.0 is a feature, and learning it now teaches you why its decisions stick. The conversation's core thesis is that Zig is countercultural: instead of stacking new abstractions on old ones, it reuses well-tested ideas and "never adds too much”. "Simple", in the Zig community's sense, means simple relative to what the machine is doing, with integer and pointer types that map closely to how you'd think about data in assembly. Chapter 6's CHIP-8 interpreter shows this: a few integers, some buffers, and elegant results. The same philosophy explains Zig's missing string type. Strings are just byte sequences with a length, and the language leaves encoding choices to you. Garrison notes that Rust, by contrast, now has to maintain its many string types forever.

Two practical takeaways for working engineers. First, allocators: because Zig encourages flat, data-oriented design, the book barely needs dynamic allocation, and when it does, allocators let you reason about memory for a whole phase of a program (say, a compiler's parser) as one unit rather than tracking the lifetime of every AST node. Second, C interop: you can use a C header directly, keep defer for cleanup instead of goto, and write small Zig wrappers around awkward C error-return conventions. The chapter on graphics and OpenGL, meanwhile, is really about a transferable systems skill: working out what an unfamiliar, committee-designed API wants from you when no tutorial exists.

items.title: Through Kazakhstan by train | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Each year, a train carrying doctors and medical gear travels through remote areas of Kazakhstan. The project is called Salamatty Kazakhstan, or "Healthy Kazakhstan." The train is underway for eight months and the clinic operates daily.

Salamatty Kazakhstan was launched by the government to improve medical care in the country's sparsely populated regions. Some communities are hundreds of kilometers from the nearest hospital or clinic. The train's timetable is shared online.

In addition to medical staff, the train crew includes kitchen staff, stewards, and technicians. On its journey of around 20,000 kilometers, the train stops in numerous villages and small towns in the Kazakh countryside. The film follows this unique social project, showing doctors and support staff as they form close bonds during the eight-month journey: working, eating and living together. Patients come to the clinic with physical ailments, but they also share their everyday worries.

The film offers a rare glimpse into this oil-rich Central Asian country. It gives viewers a sense of the respect and dedication at the heart of these special encounters between two very different worlds.

items.title: From 0 to 9 - The mysterious origins of our numbers | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Why do people in Europe refer to them as "Arabic numerals" when they were invented in India? How could ten tiny symbols conquer the world? And how did zero change the course of history?

The Western world calls them "Arabic numerals," while in the Arab world, today's European notation is thought of as being Western. What is "Arabic" about the symbols that traveled from India to Europe and on to the rest of the world?

Following the trail of our numbers leads us to Baghdad. There, in the eighth century, a scholar named al-Khwarizmi — Latinized as "Algorismi," later to be found in the word "algorithm" — helped spread Indian numerals. He would become known as the father of modern algebra. The "Arabic" numerals commonly used in Europe today derive from another variant, known as "Ghubar" — Arabic for "dust." That had emerged from the so-called "dust tables" used by Maghrebi merchants around the Mediterranean.

From Europe to America, and from the dawn of modern science to the computer age — the fascinating history of these ten small digits is enmeshed with the stories of the people who invented, spread, adopted, imposed and scrutinized them. Little by little, they have permeated every area of our lives. With the computer, numbers became the code of the modern age — and the only truly universal language.

Melting glaciers, rising sea levels, fires, floods and droughts: In 2008, with public concern about global warming on the upswing, award-winning producer and correspondent Martin Smith traveled the planet to investigate the scale of the problem, and the scale of any solution.

For years, the film reported, big businesses in the U.S. and around the globe — from oil and coal companies to electric utilities to car manufacturers — had resisted change to environmental policy and stifled the debate over climate change. But as this 2008 documentary was being made, industries and governments were facing rising pressure to reshape their approach to the environment.


To make “Heat,” Smith traveled to 12 countries on four continents, sitting down with policymakers, scientists, and leading executives from many of the largest carbon emitters from around the world, including American oil giants, Chinese coal companies, and Indian SUV makers. 


The two-hour film documented where the political and economic conversation around climate change and global warming stood in 2008, and found that some businesses were trying to fend off new regulations, while others were repositioning themselves to prosper in a world reshaped by climate change. The investigation also found that despite increasing talk about “going green,” environmental concerns were often still taking a back seat to shorter-term economic interests. And there were serious questions about the ability of industry-proposed solutions like “clean coal,” ethanol fuel subsidies, and carbon capture technology to roll back global warming. 


Editor’s note: A line of narration in this documentary cited a since-retracted assertion from the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change that "80 percent of all glacier ice in Tibet and the Himalayas will be gone by 2035." The panel attributed the statement to a media interview with a scientist who later said he had been misquoted, though the IPCC stood by its overall conclusion that “widespread mass loss from glaciers … are projected to accelerate throughout the 21st Century.”

items.title: Putin's foreign fighters - How Russia is recruiting foreign nationals for the war | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Russia needs more soldiers. At least 250,000 have already died in the Ukraine war. Moscow is also seeking new recruits abroad - sometimes using questionable methods.

A group of Indian nationals traveled to Russia for a vacation. They wound up on the front-line - conscripted against their will by the Russian army. And this is not an isolated case, with frequent reports of foreigners falling into the clutches of Russian recruiters. Russia needs a reliable supply of new soldiers for the war against Ukraine. But the Kremlin wants to avoid a mass mobilization at home. Instead, it is ramping up its international recruitment drive, targeting men from countries like Kenya, India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Cuba and Central Asia. Some are lured by money, others by promises of work or study opportunities.

Ukraine says more than 27,000 foreign fighters are now fighting on the Russian side. The film takes viewers to Ukraine, Kenya and India, features interviews with the relatives of fallen foreign soldiers, survivors and Ukrainian investigators, and reveals how Russia is exploiting economic hardship in poorer countries and, with the help of dubious intermediaries, recruiting ‘cannon fodder’ for its war against Ukraine.

items.title: The Miserable Truth About Being Queen
items.author: Weird History
items.content:
<article>Becoming a queen sounds like the ultimate fairy-tale dream: castles, crowns, lavish gowns, and absolute power. But for most history, the reality of being queen was very different. Forget the fairy tales. Royal women could face arranged marriages as teenagers, brutal childbirth, invasive royal traditions, poisonous cosmetics, filthy castles, and bizarre court customs that would horrify us today.

On this episode of Weird History, we uncover the shocking, disgusting, and downright bizarre reality of what it was really like to be a queen in the past, from forced marriages and public births to lead-based makeup and nobles using fireplaces as toilets, life inside a medieval palace was anything but glamorous.

items.title: Mao Zedong - From peasants' son to communist revolutionary (1/3) | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>From peasants' son to revolutionary leader — Mao Zedong laid the foundation for modern China. This three-part documentary offers an in-depth look at one of the most influential figures of the 20th century. *Part 2 & 3 coming soon!*

Part 2: Available from 10 October 2026
Part 3: Available from 17 October 2026

The legacy of the "founding father" of the People's Republic of China remains deeply controversial. Revered in Europe as a revolutionary icon in the late 1960s, Mao led China to the brink of disaster and ultimately clung to power with a regime of terror. Yet today's leaders in Beijing continue to draw on the cult of Mao. China is now a global power, a transformation that would be difficult to imagine without Mao Zedong.

When Mao Zedong was born in 1893, nothing hinted at his meteoric rise to power. The son of a farming family, he grew up during a period of political instability and profound social upheaval. The 1911 Revolution, which marked the beginning of the end of imperial rule, awakened his mind to politics. At first, Mao had no clear political program. But the Russian Revolution of 1917 introduced him to Marxist ideas, and he soon became a co-founder of the Communist Party of China.

Mao rose steadily through the party ranks as conflict with the nationalist Kuomintang party intensified into a bloody civil war. The devastating retreat that became known as the "Long March" went down in history to become the foundation of the cult of Mao. After World War II, the struggle for power in China continued until Mao and his forces finally reached Beijing.

This three-part series traces Mao Zedong's journey from peasants' son to revolutionary and architect of modern China — from his rural childhood to the founding of the People's Republic to the devastating impact of the Cultural Revolution in the 1960s, which claimed millions of lives.

Archival footage, as well as interviews with historians and eyewitnesses, tell the story of the man who changed China forever.

items.title: Turkey's $20 Billion Fund Collapse Explained
items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:
<article>Get an exclusive 15% discount on Saily data plans! Use code BOYLE at checkout. Download Saily app or go to https://www.saily.com/boyle

In September 2026, Turkey's investment fund industry collapsed, after funds run by Tera and Pusula failed to meet redemptions and regulators froze and liquidated 131 funds holding about $20 billion of savings belonging to more than 455,000 investors. In this video, Patrick Boyle looks at how Emre Tezmen's Tera, which hoped to become "the Goldman Sachs of Turkey," reported returns of more than 66,000%, how funds buying thinly traded Borsa Istanbul stocks allegedly inflated their own valuations, and how money market funds that savers treated as cash ended up exposed to inflated shares through reverse repo loans. We also cover the warnings from MSCI and Turkey's finance minister, the arrests and political fallout from what Turkey's justice minister has called "Ponzi-like schemes," what Bernie Cornfeld's Investors Overseas Services and Bill Hwang's Archegos Capital tell us about market manipulation and leverage, and why weak institutions and tiny fines let bad actors drive out honest businesses. Along the way, we try to track down the "notorious malevolent forces" that Tezmen blamed for the collapse.

items.author: BBC Earth Science
items.content:
<article>The Sun can unleash colossal storms of charged particles that hurtle through space at incredible speeds. They can disrupt satellites and infrastructure, and even put human life at risk. items.title: Trump and power - A deep divide across America | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>A cinematic journey through the first year of Donald Trump's second term as president. Fear, hope, protest, loyalty and disappointment all shape this portrait of the US as a nation in turmoil.

Washington, D.C., and Piedmont, West Virginia. As President Trump's second term sparks fear and alarm in the liberal capital, coal country in Appalachia clings to the hope of a long-awaited economic turnaround.

Only a two-and-a-half-hour drive separates Washington, D.C., from Piedmont, West Virginia — yet the two places exist in hugely different cultural worlds. In liberal D.C., shock about Donald Trump's return for a second term runs deep. Many federal workers fear for their jobs, rights and democracy. In coal country, by contrast, Trump is seen as the last hope for an economic revival. Coal trains may still rumble through town, but factories stand empty and drug problems are tearing through the community. Even so, there's tremendous resilience to be found here.

This documentary follows both places over the course of a year, exploring how people with sharply contrasting realities see Trump's return to the presidency. In Washington, D.C., guerrilla artist Robin Bell uses nighttime video projections to send a message of resistance. In doing so, he becomes a barometer for freedom of expression. In Piedmont, the filmmakers meet former corrections officer and pastor Dave Cowan — a pragmatic man of faith who fears the decline of America while also remaining hopeful that things will finally change.

Filmed up close with the people at the heart of these communities and complemented by the voices of historians, democracy experts and Christian conservatives, the journey follows the first 365 days of Donald Trump's second term as president — and offers a glimpse of what may yet lie ahead.

items.title: How new wearable tech is changing horse racing
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>Horse racing can be an unusually dangerous profession for both the jockey and the horse: Riding a half-ton animal at nearly 40 miles per hour means your fate depends on the health and performance of both athletes. And the horse can be at risk of catastrophic injury if the jockey doesn’t have the required physical fitness to maintain proper technique and lightning-quick reflexes. 

But new wearable technology and advances in sports medicine are enabling everyone involved in the sport of horse racing to identify risks earlier and prevent injuries to horses and jockeys alike.

In order to find out more about both of these athletes, Vox producer Nate Krieger took a trip to Belmont Park, to watch competitive horses train and to speak with Dr. Sara Langsam, an equine veterinarian and chair of the American Association of Equine Practitioners Racing Committee. And to learn about the jockey side of the equation, he talked to Michaela Keener, a jockey health researcher at University of Kentucky, and ReyLu Gutiérrez, a jockey who has started in over 6,000 races.

items.title: Rudolf Steiner and his Waldorf philosophy | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Rudolf Steiner is synonymous with Waldorf education - and its controversial teachings. This documentary explores the impact his ideas have had, and why they continue to draw both supporters and critics, to this day.

The name Rudolf Steiner resonates. To some, he's a visionary educational reformer and humanist. To others, the founder of a world view that lies beyond scientific validity. His teachings have shaped education, agriculture and medicine - garnering plenty of criticism, along the way.

The film paints a nuanced portrait of a thinker vacillating between a desire for reform and esotericism. It explores the enduring impact of his ideas and asks what role they play in the present day, at a time when scientific knowledge and social norms are increasingly coming into question. Does Steiner's esoteric world view help fuel today's skepticism towards science?

<article>Millions of Americans have fallen victim to a growing epidemic of online scams — from sextortion schemes aimed at teens, to crypto investment scams targeting seniors. What’s behind the rise?

FRONTLINE and The Associated Press have spent more than a year investigating the shadowy world of online scams, and how this global criminal industry is stealing billions of dollars each year. The 90-minute documentary “Scammed” goes inside the explosive growth of an industry powered in many cases by organized crime, trafficked labor, American technology, and, increasingly, AI — and how governments and law enforcement have tried to keep pace. 

Drawing on interviews with perpetrators, victims and officials, as well as thousands of never-before-seen documents, “Scammed” pieces together a look inside the global scam industry — from sextortion scams run from Nigeria, to massive scam compounds in Southeast Asia that rely on human trafficking for labor — and the underlying technologies and platforms being used to scam victims in the U.S. and worldwide. The documentary also examines why so few people ever get their money back.

items.title: High-tech shark deterrence - Australia's new strategy for safe beaches | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>After a series of fatal shark attacks, Australia is turning toward high-tech solutions. This includes drones, smart capture systems and cutting-edge research, which — unlike shark nets — don't harm the predatory fish.

Marine biologist Paul Butcher heads the New South Wales shark management program, which introduced smart drumlines that allow sharks to be caught alive before being tagged and released without hurting them. The program is aided by the world's largest drone-based beach surveillance system.

One of Butcher's key collaborators is Mark Atkins, who oversees the drone program. The system delivers real-time warnings for swimmers and surfers, while airborne cameras also provide researchers with valuable data on shark movements. 

Drone operator Gabriel Roxburgh conducts patrols of Bellina's coastline. He is taking a closer look at the new arrival of massive schools of baitfish, because he knows that, where prey gathers, large predators usually follow.

But the high-tech approach also has its critics. Surfer and shark-control activist Daniel Webber says stronger measures are needed, and that the move away from traditional shark nets puts human lives at risk. In neighboring Queensland, those nets are still widely used — despite their impact on sea turtles, dolphins and other marine life. Environmental activists like Brylee Robinson and marine biologist Bella Graham are fighting for them to be banned.

The documentary explores the tensions between public safety and wildlife conservation, as well as technological innovation and political pressure — a delicate balancing act centering on the question of whether humans and sharks can peacefully coexist.

items.title: The Mysteries of Ancient Ireland | Full Series
items.author: History Hit
items.content:
<article>We explored the ancient sites of Ireland. 

Tristan Hughes explores the ancient myths that surround Stone Age Ireland and uncovers Ireland’s prehistoric metal revolution, the Bronze Age. 

In episode 1 Tristan visits the Brú na Bóinne complex, which holds some of the most extraordinary structures of the prehistoric world. Tristan travels to Ireland to delve into the mysteries of Newgrange and its surrounding tombs — exploring the secrets of Stone Age Ireland. Along the way, he gets up close to artefacts uncovered from the tombs, examines the breathtaking rock art carved into their stones, and investigates the myths and beliefs that have echoed through this sacred landscape for over 5,000 years.

A UNESCO World Heritage Site, Brú na Bóinne sits on the north bank of the River Boyne and is dominated by the world-famous passage tombs of Newgrange, Knowth, and Dowth. Older than the Great Pyramids of Giza, these monumental structures date back to the Neolithic Period, which began around 4000 BC. 

Newgrange has long been a centre of spiritual, astrological, and ceremonial significance — a sacred place where the natural world was revered and influential individuals were honoured in death.

In episode 2, Tristan traverses Ireland, exploring a golden age of transformation, Ireland’s Bronze Age. Copper mining started in Ireland around 2400 BC, in the Chalcolithic, or copper age, the period between the end of the Stone Age and the Bronze age. Tristan climbs Mount Gabriel in County Cork to investigate Bronze Age Copper mines. Ireland’s ‘copper craze’ continued for generations, but it wasn’t just copper that was found here, they also mined for gold! Tristan explores the beautifully intricate golden Lunula. Special boats and trackways appeared all over Ireland connecting these new bronze age billionaires to the wider prehistoric world. 

Tristan visits one of these trackways at Craggaunowen before getting hands on helping out with daily life. One of the most extraordinary legacies of Bronze Age Ireland are Fulacht Fiadh or burnt mounds, which are most probably ceremonial cooking sites, and Tristan gets to see one in action. But life in Bronze Age Ireland wasn’t all idyllic countryside cooking - by the middle of the Bronze Age defensive hillforts began to arise. Rathgall Hillfort epitomises this, it was a centre of defense, community, trade and the forging of weapons, tools and artefacts.

items.title: India's little-known minority - The Siddi and the Olympic dream | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Nimeksha Siddi is 18 years old and India's sprinting hope for the 2028 Olympics. Nimeksha belongs to the Siddi ethnic group, whose daily lives are marked by racism and exclusion.

The 18-year-old sprinter Nimeksha flies down the home straight like a bolt of lightning. She's a Siddi. Hardly anyone knows about her people, not even in India, where the Siddi have lived for 500 years. Her ancestors came to India from Africa as slaves or mercenaries. It's not known how many Siddi live in India. They all have the surname Siddi. They are Muslim, Christian or Hindu - and are often mistaken for tourists by many Indians. Most live in poverty, scraping by as day laborers, gathering plants, honey or rubber.

In 1983, India's Minister for Sport launched a program aimed at tapping into the community's athletic potential. Children from Siddi villages were recruited and coached in running. One of the most successful was Kamala Siddi. At the age of 15, she set a national record in the pentathlon, won bronze and gold at international level, and was rewarded with a job on the railways and a flat with running water.

Now her daughter Nimeksha is in the spotlight. She could become India's hope for the 2028 Olympic Games.

items.title: How dependent is Germany on skilled workers from abroad? | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>To what extent do German hospitals rely on foreign healthcare professionals? This film looks at expert opinions and the personal experiences of doctors from abroad, to highlight the structural challenges facing the German hospital system.

Germany is training more doctors than ever before - but the shortfall in hospitals still runs to thousands. The reason for this lies less in the absolute figures than in their distribution. Many specialists are drawn to urban centers, while rural areas face a shortage of skilled staff. Furthermore, many doctors are set to retire in the coming years, and an increasing number of them are working part-time. This is creating a noticeable shortage despite the high density of doctors, a problem exacerbated by a hospital system that's under financial pressure in many places. 

Although Germany has many hospitals by international standards, these include numerous small clinics in rural areas that are often barely profitable. To counteract this trend, a comprehensive hospital reform was launched at the end of 2024: fewer sites, greater specialization, and more outpatient treatment. While the Joint Federal Committee sees opportunities for greater efficiency in this move, the German Hospital Association warns that new gaps in care could arise in rural areas.

The documentary follows Mohamed Cherbagi, an internist from Syria who most recently worked at a hospital in Freiberg, Saxony, and Ina Viaroukina from Belarus, a junior doctor at the Harzklinikum in Quedlinburg. Both are taking on roles in places where their German colleagues are becoming increasingly hard to find. Through their personal stories, along with insightful commentary from experts, the documentary shows just how dependent many hospitals are on doctors from abroad, and how this dependence is linked to the structural challenges facing the German hospital system.

items.title: C++26 for Lazy Programmers • Will Briggs & Todd Montgomery • GOTO 2026
items.author: GOTO Conferences
items.content:
<article>This interview was recorded for the GOTO Book Club. #GOTOcon #GOTObookclub
http://gotopia.tech/bookclub

Check out more here:
https://gotopia.tech/episodes/454

Will Briggs - Professor of Computer Science at University of Lynchburg & Author of "C++26 for Lazy Programmers"
Todd L. Montgomery - Software Professional & Advisor at DRW & Co-Author & Co-Maintainer of Aeron, Agrona & Simple Binary Encoding (SBE) 

RESOURCES
Will
https://www.linkedin.com/in/will-briggs-32635714a
https://www.lynchburg.edu/will-briggs

Todd
https://twitter.com/toddlmontgomery
https://www.linkedin.com/in/todd-montgomery-413a3216
https://github.com/tmontgomery

DESCRIPTION
Will Briggs — a University of Lynchburg computer science professor with three decades of experience teaching C++ — joins Todd L. Montgomery to talk through C++26 for Lazy Programmers, and the conversation opens on the question every language-learning book has to answer right now: does learning a language still matter when AI writes so much of the code?
Briggs' answer is refreshingly unhyped — he tests a new AI tool about once a year on a real, medium-difficulty problem, and as of this year's attempt, it still couldn't solve one, though it's genuinely useful for speeding up work he already understands. Both he and Montgomery land on the same practical conclusion: reading code fluently matters more now, not less, because code is increasingly how AI communicates back to you, and you can't debug or direct what you can't read. The rest of the conversation is a genuine craft discussion about how to teach C++ well — sequencing concepts so a beginner never has to hold two new ideas at once, giving double duty to topics like operator overloading and custom string classes, and deliberately introducing pointers nineteen chapters before ever using the word "pointer", by building the underlying mental model through arrays first.

For engineers who've been away from C++ or are watching it from a distance, there are a few sharp, specific takeaways: Briggs points to AI-generated C++ as noticeably more reliable than AI-generated Java, plausibly because of training-corpus quality rather than anything about the language itself, and he's blunt about C++26's biggest usability problem being proliferation, not power — he cites a case of 25 different ways floating around online just to initialize a single number, and argues the language needs fewer new ways to do old things. He also makes a case, backed by the TIOBE index, that C — a language from 1972 — is still the second most popular language in the world, and that learning C++ specifically (precisely because it's hard and concept-dense) is some of the best preparation available for picking up nearly any other language quickly afterward.

items.title: Life on the autism spectrum (2/2) | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>People on the autism spectrum have dreams like many other people’s: love, a career, friendships. But the path to achieving them is often strewn with challenges.

"Life on the Spectrum" tells the stories of Sebastian, Lena, Diane and Elias. With sensitivity and intimacy, it shows us just how varied and complicated life with autism can be. There’s Sebastian, who's looking for a partner. Lena wants to become a doctor, despite all the setbacks she has faced. And Diane, who wants to help her son Elias settle into school life, but keeps encountering obstacles in the process. They offer us moving insights into their lives at these pivotal moments.

The documentary doesn't focus on the diagnosis, but rather on the people themselves, with their hopes, strengths and vulnerabilities. With a gentle camera style and a visual language that also brings inner landscapes to life, the documentary opens doors to a world that's still unfamiliar to many.

<article>This interview was recorded for the GOTO Book Club. #GOTOcon #GOTObookclub
http://gotopia.tech/bookclub

https://youtu.be/mRoWGqcBSzk

DESCRIPTION
Kaspar von Grünberg and Luca Galante — co-authors of the new book Thinking in Platforms and co-founders of Humanitec and the PlatformEngineering.org community — trace their field back to an origin story most engineers will recognize: a company held hostage by a single backend engineer who could threaten to walk unless he got a 3x raise. That "key person dependency" problem, they argue, is exactly what industrialization solved a century earlier when Henry Ford moved manufacturing from artisan workshops to standardized assembly lines — and it's the same move platform engineering makes for software: treating the internal setup as a product instead of something that "just happens" to a team. The book is structured in three parts — historical foundations, a "path-to-outcome" conceptual framework built around golden paths, and a hands-on playbook for going from a minimum viable platform to full enterprise adoption — because, as they note, most platform efforts don't fail on the technical side; they fail on the social side, in getting buy-in from developers, executives, and security teams alike.

The conversation's sharpest point for engineers building with AI right now: agents make platforms non-optional, not less necessary. An AI agent dropped into an enterprise full of undocumented "tribal knowledge" fails for the same reason a new hire would — except at scale, and fast. Von Grünberg's analogy: it's like hiring a brilliant intern and sending them into an office where nobody speaks their language, then being surprised there's no output a week later. That means real infrastructure — context management, security, observability, governance — has to exist before agents can be productive, and the old rule of thumb that you needed 100+ developers to justify a platform team no longer applies when a single person can be running a thousand agents. The bigger claim: platform engineering is already spreading past IT into security, data, and eventually every knowledge-work function, becoming less a software discipline and more the operating model for AI-first organizations.

items.title: The Biggest Oil Spill You’ve Probably Never Heard Of | Spain: The Lawless Sea | FRONTLINE/World
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>How an aging tanker caused one of Spain’s worst environmental disasters — and what it revealed about maritime regulations. (Aired January 2004)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate
In November 2002, the oil tanker “Prestige” sank off the coast of Galicia in northwestern Spain after encountering a winter storm, causing one of the worst oil spills in the country’s history.

The tanker had a murky and complicated backstory — making it difficult to track culpability. At 26 years old, the rusting, single-hulled tanker was well past the age of retirement. But that didn’t deter the owners from loading the aging ship with crude oil number 4, one of the most toxic fuel oils known.

After the spill, Spain imposed a six-month ban on fishing in the region, leading to great economic hardship.

“Spain: The Lawless Sea” investigated what went wrong with the tanker and uncovered a largely unregulated maritime system that offered few safeguards against environmental disasters.

“This is an act of terror, a criminal act,” said Rafael Mouzo, a fisherman and then-mayor of the coastal town of Concurbion. “We need an international tribunal to judge ... all those responsible for the spill.”

Learn about developments since the film aired on our website:

items.title: Rivers under pressure - From drought and competing agendas | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>Hotter temperatures, falling groundwater levels, and dry soil are putting pressure on Germany's water resources. Can plans to improve water retention and restore river landscapes solve the problem?

This documentary follows people who are fighting to secure the future of water resources in three German states. They range from scientists to farmers, to environmental groups, and politicians. 

We discover the consequences of decades of river straightening and hear why floodplains are so important for flood protection, drinking water supply, and climate adaptation. Using the examples of the Unstrut, Mulde, and Elbe rivers, the film illustrates the opportunities offered by renaturation projects as well as the divisions they can cause. Amid the tensions between nature conservation, agriculture, and political interests, one central question arises: How can Germany ensure more water is retained in the land in future?

items.title: Where Does the Quantum World End and Ours Begin? | PODCAST: The Joy of Why
items.author: Quanta Magazine
items.content:
<article>Jonathan Halliwell explains how quantum decoherence is key to understanding how we transition from a world with a wave-like nature of matter and energy to the classical macroscopic world that we’re used to.

“The Joy of Why” is a Quanta Magazine podcast about curiosity and the pursuit of knowledge. The mathematician and author Steven Strogatz and the cosmologist and author Janna Levin take turns interviewing leading researchers about the great scientific and mathematical questions of our time.  For more episodes visit Quanta Magazine: https://www.quantamagazine.org/tag/the-joy-of-why/

--------

0:00 Why Quantum Mechanics Remains a Mystery
2:17 Applying Quantum Physics to the Universe
6:55 Schrödinger’s Cat and the Double-Slit Experiment
10:51 Is Everything Fundamentally a Wave?
12:15 How the Quantum World Becomes Classical
18:38 Does Consciousness Affect Quantum Mechanics?
22:40 Is the Moon There When No One Is Looking?
29:29 Does Measuring a System Change It?
34:00 Why Keep Testing Quantum Mechanics?
37:22 Learning to Live With Scientific Mystery

---------

Quantum mechanics may be one of the most precisely tested paradigms in science, but there’s still no universally accepted interpretation of what it tells us about reality. How do we get from the wave-like behavior of quantum systems to the solid, macroscopic world of objects and the universe at large?

Jonathan Halliwell, a professor of theoretical physics at Imperial College London, has spent his career probing the foundations of quantum theory. In this episode, he tells Steven Strogatz why decoherence — the process by which fragile quantum behavior becomes dispersed through interactions with the surrounding environment — is key to the transition from quantum to classical behavior, and he describes the “histories” approach that he uses to understand this. Along the way, Halliwell tackles some of the field’s deepest paradoxes. He explains why the quantum-to-classical transition doesn’t require a conscious observer, and he explores Einstein’s famous question of whether the moon is really there when no one looks. The conversation ends with Halliwell explaining how yoga and meditation help him sit with the mystery of competing perspectives in science.

items.title: How India's Day Retail Traders Lost Billions
items.author: Bloomberg Originals
items.content:
<article>Today's financial markets operate at lightning speed, dominated by algorithms and high-frequency trading firms. Nowhere has the impact of this technological advantage been more visible than in India, the world’s largest options trading hub. 

Fueled by mobile apps and so-called finfluencers, millions of everyday investors flooded the market, only to lose billions of dollars while global HFT firms raked in massive profits. Now, as Indian regulators scrutinize the trading of one of those firms, Jane Street, a critical question emerges: should ultra-fast automated trading be seen as an engine for efficient markets, or a game stacked against the average investor?
